title: Built-in Algorithms
relevance: STL <algorithm> and <numeric> routines are expected in C++ interviews and OAs; using them correctly saves time and avoids hand-rolled loop bugs.

phases.goal: Establish what core <algorithm>/<numeric> facilities exist and what each one returns or mutates.

must_hit.point: std::sort is an O(n log n) comparison-based sort, typically Introsort (Quicksort, Heapsort, and Insertion Sort).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names sort’s class (comparison-based O(n log n)) and mentions Introsort or the three hybrid pieces.

must_hit.point: A comparator is a boolean callable on (a, b) that returns true iff a must appear strictly before b in the sorted order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the strict-before contract, not a vague “returns whether a is smaller.”

must_hit.point: lower_bound returns the first element not less than (>=) val; upper_bound returns the first strictly greater than (>) val.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both iterator semantics with >= vs > wording.

must_hit.point: equal_range returns the half-open [lower_bound, upper_bound) of elements equivalent to val.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the pair of iterators as that half-open span.

must_hit.point: unique and remove only rearrange and return a new logical end; they do not resize—pair with erase (erase-unique / erase-remove).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions no resize / new logical end and the erase pairing idioms.

probes: What does std::sort guarantee about time and typical implementation, and how do you express a custom order?
What do lower_bound and upper_bound each return on a sorted range?

hints.1: Think iterators and ordering contracts, not just “sort the vector.”
hints.2: Sort: O(n log n) Introsort; comparator means strictly before; bounds are first >= vs first >.
hints.3: sort is O(n log n) Introsort; comparator returns true if a must precede b; lower_bound = first not less than val, upper_bound = first strictly greater; unique/remove need erase to shrink.

phases.goal: Check how complexities, iterator categories, and ordering rules make these algorithms correct or wrong.

must_hit.point: A custom comparator must enforce strict weak ordering and return false for identical/equivalent elements; returning a <= b instead of a < b is undefined behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links non-strict <= to UB / crash risk under strict weak ordering.

must_hit.point: nth_element places the correct element at the k-th position as if fully sorted; elements before are ≤ it and after are ≥ it, in O(n) average time (QuickSelect).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States k-th position guarantee, ≤/≥ partition, and O(n) average QuickSelect.

must_hit.point: partial_sort makes the first k elements the smallest k in sorted order in O(n log k); is_sorted checks sortedness in O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both algorithms’ roles and those complexities from the notes.

must_hit.point: Binary search algorithms are O(log n) for random-access iterators; on std::set/map you must use member lower_bound/upper_bound because free std::lower_bound is O(n) on non-random-access iterators while members are O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts free O(n) on trees vs member O(log n), and RA O(log n) baseline.

must_hit.point: make_heap is O(n); push_heap and pop_heap are O(log n) and require push_back before push_heap and pop_back after pop_heap; sort_heap sorts a heap ascending in O(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites those complexities and the push_back/pop_back choreography.

must_hit.point: Set algebra algorithms need two sorted ranges, write via an output iterator, and run in O(N + M).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions sorted inputs, output iterator (e.g. back_inserter), and O(N + M).

probes: Why can a comparator written with <= crash sort, and what must it guarantee?
Why must you call set/map member lower_bound instead of std::lower_bound on the tree?

hints.1: Ordering and iterator category drive both correctness and asymptotic cost.
hints.2: Strict weak ordering forbids <= on equals; tree free algorithms walk linearly; heap helpers need the push/pop vector steps.
hints.3: <= in a comparator is UB; nth_element is O(n) average QuickSelect with ≤/≥ sides; free lower_bound on set/map is O(n) vs member O(log n); make_heap O(n), push/pop_heap O(log n).

phases.goal: Choose among related STL tools when stability, access to storage, or evaluation order matters.

must_hit.point: stable_sort preserves relative order of equivalent elements (useful for multi-key passes) and is O(n log^2 n), or O(n log n) with enough extra memory, unlike ordinary sort.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names stability use-case and the two complexity cases from the notes.

must_hit.point: Manual heap on a vector (make_heap and friends) vs priority_queue: use the vector heap when you need to inspect the underlying array or build a heap in O(n) in place without copying.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties manual heap to inspectability and O(n) in-place build.

must_hit.point: reduce is like accumulate but may evaluate out of order (C++17, for parallelism); accumulate’s init type fixes the accumulation type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts out-of-order reduce with typed accumulate init.

probes: When would you pick stable_sort over sort, and what complexity should you quote?
When is a manual heap on a vector preferable to priority_queue?

hints.1: Stability, memory, and whether you need the container layout are the levers.
hints.2: stable_sort keeps equivalent order; vector heap exposes storage and O(n) make_heap; reduce relaxes order vs accumulate.
hints.3: stable_sort: preserve equivalent order, O(n log^2 n) or O(n log n) with extra memory; make_heap for O(n) in-place inspectable heap; reduce allows out-of-order vs accumulate’s init-typed sum.

phases.goal: Apply standard idioms and numeric/bit pitfalls the way interview/OA code expects.

must_hit.point: To generate all permutations: sort first, then process in a do/while driven by next_permutation (O(n) per call); false means it wrapped to the lexicographically smallest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sort-then-next_permutation loop and wrap-around meaning of false.

must_hit.point: Count equals on a sorted vector via upper_bound index minus lower_bound index (iterators converted with it - v.begin()).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses bound difference after converting iterators to indices.

must_hit.point: Pass 0LL (not 0) as accumulate’s init when the sum may overflow a 32-bit integer, because init’s type dictates the sum type.
__builtin_clz(0) and __builtin_ctz(0) are undefined behavior—check x != 0 first; abs(INT_MIN) is also UB from overflow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions both zero-arg builtin UB and abs(INT_MIN).

must_hit.point: Avoid std::pow for integer powers (e.g. inaccuracies that truncate wrong); use 1LL << k for powers of two or iterative modular exponentiation in O(log exp).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects pow for ints and names bit-shift or modexp alternative.

probes: Show the idiom to enumerate all permutations of a vector with next_permutation.
How do you safely sum a vector of ints that might overflow 32-bit with accumulate?

hints.1: Interview code leans on erase idioms, bounds arithmetic, and typed accumulate.
hints.2: Sort then next_permutation; ub-lb for counts; 0LL init; guard clz/ctz and INT_MIN abs.
hints.3: do { … } while (next_permutation(...)) after sort; count = (upper_bound - begin) - (lower_bound - begin); accumulate(..., 0LL); never clz/ctz(0); prefer 1LL << k or modexp over pow.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use sort for default O(n log n) unordered ties among equals; use stable_sort when equivalent elements must keep relative order across multi-criteria passes, accepting O(n log^2 n) or O(n log n) if enough extra memory is available.

tradeoffs.topic: std::lower_bound free function vs set/map member lower_bound
tradeoffs.strong_answer: On vectors/arrays (random-access), free lower_bound/upper_bound are O(log n). On std::set/map, free std::lower_bound is O(n) because iterators are not random-access; call the container’s member lower_bound/upper_bound for O(log n).

tradeoffs.topic: priority_queue vs manual heap on a vector
tradeoffs.strong_answer: priority_queue is the usual interface; make_heap/push_heap/pop_heap/sort_heap when you need to inspect the underlying array or build a heap in O(n) directly on an existing vector without copying.
accumulate folds with a typed init (init type is the sum type). reduce (C++17) is similar but may evaluate out of order, enabling parallelism.

gotchas.trap: Writing a comparator with a <= b (or otherwise returning true for equivalent elements).
gotchas.correction: Comparators must implement strict weak ordering and return false for identical/equivalent elements; use strict < style predicates or sort hits undefined behavior (often a segfault).

gotchas.trap: Calling std::lower_bound / std::upper_bound on a std::set or std::map.
gotchas.correction: Use the member .lower_bound() / .upper_bound(); free algorithms are O(n) on bidirectional tree iterators, members are O(log n).

gotchas.trap: Expecting unique or remove to shrink the container by themselves.
gotchas.correction: They only compact and return the new logical end; finish with erase (erase-unique / erase-remove). For unique, sort first if duplicates are not already consecutive.

gotchas.trap: accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) when the sum can exceed 32-bit range.
gotchas.correction: Init type controls the accumulation type—pass 0LL so the sum is long long.
Those are undefined behavior; always ensure x != 0 first.

gotchas.trap: Using abs(INT_MIN), or std::pow / floating sqrt for exact integer results.
gotchas.correction: abs(INT_MIN) overflows (UB). Prefer integer methods or careful rounding for roots; for powers of two use 1LL << k, otherwise iterative modular exponentiation—not std::pow on doubles.
